title: God Heard the Voice of the Boy — Laughter, Casting Out, a Well
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. The man we followed last lesson had already been walking with God for twenty-five years, and we watched him drop back into the very same pit he had fallen into before; and we watched God refuse to replace him over it — God even sent the king he had deceived to go and ask that same man to pray for him.
And the first sentence of this chapter is this: "Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said."
The chapter that comes straight after his fall is the chapter in which the promise is kept.

So let me ask you something first. That thing you are waiting for — how long have you been waiting now? Three years? Ten? Long enough that you have stopped bringing it up in front of other people, because you are embarrassed to?

Let me put the answer at the very front. The promise looks twenty-five years late, and in fact it was not out by a single day. And in the hour when hope has run out, what we need most is very often not a change in our circumstances. It is a pair of eyes being opened.
1. At the Set Time of Which God Had Spoken

Verses 1 and 2: "Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said, and Yahweh did to Sarah as he had spoken. Sarah conceived, and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him."
Brothers and sisters, there are several words inside those two verses that you have to see clearly.

The first is "visited", פָּקַד (*paqad*). You have met the same use of it back in chapter 8 — it does not mean "to call something to mind"; it means "to step in and deal with it". In Exodus 3:16 God says, "I have surely visited you, and seen that which is done to you in Egypt"; Ruth 1:6 says that Naomi had heard "how Yahweh had visited his people in giving them bread". Wherever this word appears, it means God has started to move.

The second is "as he had said" and "as he had spoken". In one verse the same thing is pressed home twice running, and with two different verbs. The author is doing it deliberately: this happened exactly the way he said it would.

The third, and the weightiest of the three: "at the set time of which God had spoken", לַמּוֹעֵד (*lamo'ed*). The word means an appointed festival, a fixed appointment, a time agreed on beforehand. God had already named it once in 17:21 — "whom Sarah will bear to you at this set time next year" — and named it again in 18:14: "At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes around, and Sarah will have a son."
Brothers and sisters, take this one in carefully. Seen from where a human being stands, this is twenty-five years overdue. Seen from where the text stands, this is called the set time.
Twenty-five years is not a delay. It is an itinerary.

And let me be honest with you: that is an easy thing to say from a pulpit and a very hard thing to believe inside the waiting. Because across those twenty-five years there was not one single year in which somebody stood next to them and said, "This is part of the itinerary." All you ever know is that another year has gone.

So look at the way the text is written. It does not record a single one of the disappointments of those twenty-five years; it goes straight to the fulfilment. And Scripture is able to write like that because it is looking back from the far end. You are standing in the middle of it. You cannot see that shape from where you are, and that is entirely normal.
"At the set time of which God had spoken" — why does the text go out of its way to stress that phrase?

Verse 2 says, "Sarah conceived, and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him." Twenty-five years of waiting are gathered up and stored inside those few words: the set time of which God had spoken. The text does not say "at last". It does not say "after all that struggle". It says only that the day had come. That way of writing is correcting something in us. We assume God is dragging his feet; in fact he is keeping an appointment. For anyone who is in the middle of waiting, that carries two things. First, there is a date — it is not open-ended. Second, the date is the one God named, not the one we set. And here is a small practice you can actually do: write down the thing you are waiting for, and write beside it, "at the set time of which God has spoken".
2. God Made a Laugh for Her
Verse 6: "Sarah said, 'God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me.'"

Brothers and sisters, this verse is extraordinarily beautiful in Hebrew. "Laughter" here, צְחֹק (*tsechoq*), is a noun and not a verb; and the verb behind "has made me" is עָשָׂה (*asah*) — to make, to fashion, to manufacture.
So word for word it runs like this: "God has made a laugh for me."
The laughter is something God made with his own hands.

Now put that sentence down beside 18:12. In chapter 18 she "laughed within herself" inside the tent — the bitter little laugh of a woman who has waited far too long and has already shut the door on the subject; and afterwards she even denied it: "I didn't laugh."
In chapter 21, with the child in her arms, she says, "God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me."

The same root, and two entirely different sounds. One laugh is behind a closed door and will not own its own name; the other wants the whole world to laugh along with it. Between the two of them lies one year — and a God who asks, "Is anything too hard for Yahweh?"

And the child's name is Isaac, יִצְחָק (*Yitschaq*) — "he laughs". Brothers and sisters, God did not delete their laughter. He wrote that laugh into the name of the son of the promise, and then he rewrote what was inside it.

Verse 4 says, "Abraham circumcised his son, Isaac, when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him." "As God had commanded him" — you have seen this piece of commentary before, in 17:23, where he did it "as God had said to him". The same verdict, written over this man for the second time. There are real failures in this man's life; and this sentence keeps coming back too.
"God has made me laugh" — how is this laugh different from the laughs before it?

One root (צָחַק) and three laughs. In chapter 17 Abraham's laugh has disbelief in it — he falls on his face and laughs at the thought of a hundred-year-old man having a son. In chapter 18 Sarah's laugh has self-mockery in it, laughing at herself inside the tent. And in chapter 21 Sarah says, "God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me." God did not take the laugh away. He changed what was inside it. And there is a lovely detail buried in the sentence: "Everyone who hears will laugh with me" — her joy is not shut behind a door, it is meant to be handed round. Which says something to us: the restoration God gives you is usually meant for other people as well. If your story has no outlet, that joy will slowly dry out.
A great feast on the day Isaac was weaned — was a celebration on that scale really necessary?

In that world a child was weaned at around two or three years old, and that marked the end of the stretch when infant mortality was at its highest — so the day was, in effect, the day everyone could finally say, "He really has survived." Throwing a feast is the act of taking a private mercy and turning it into a public testimony. And that is still worth learning today. We are thoroughly used to saying our hardships out loud so that people will pray, and we very rarely say the answered things out loud so that people can hear them. Scripture's practice is to do both. Here is a practical suggestion: if there has been one thing God has done for you this year, find an occasion, put a meal on the table, and tell the story. A testimony is not showing off. A testimony is handing the glory back.
3. A Light from the Original: the Eyes That Were Opened

After verse 8 the camera suddenly darkens. On the day Isaac was weaned Abraham made a great feast; and Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian "mocking" — and that word for mocking, מְצַחֵק (*metsacheq*), is once again built on the root "laugh". A third laugh, inside the same chapter.
And so Sarah says, "Cast out this servant and her son!"
Verse 11: "The thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight on account of his son." The Hebrew is very heavy indeed — וַיֵּרַע מְאֹד (*vayera meod*), in his eyes this thing was exceedingly evil.

And then in verse 12 God says, "Don't let it be grievous in your sight because of the boy, and because of your servant. In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice. For your offspring will be named through Isaac." And verse 13 comes immediately after it: "I will also make a nation of the son of the servant, because he is your child."

Brothers and sisters, we have to make a very careful distinction here. What God endorses is the outcome of that decision — the line of the promise runs through Isaac. But who created this whole situation in the first place? It was Sarai's own arrangement back in chapter 16. God here is clearing up the wreckage; he is not signing off on the method that produced it. And notice that in the same breath he immediately promises to protect the child who is being sent away.

Verse 14: "Abraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread and a container of water, and gave it to Hagar." "Rose up early in the morning", וַיַּשְׁכֵּם בַּבֹּקֶר (*vayashkem baboqer*) — this is the third time the phrase turns up in Genesis about this man. In 19:27 he went up early in the morning and saw the smoke going up from the plain; in 21:14 he rises early in the morning to send a woman and a child away; in 22:3 he rises early in the morning to go and offer Isaac. Brothers and sisters, all three times it is a hard thing. Rising early in the morning is this man's way of facing what is hard.

And then comes the wilderness. Verses 15 and 16: "The water in the container was spent, and she put the child under one of the shrubs. She went and sat down opposite him, a good way off, about a bow shot away. For she said, 'Don't let me see the death of the child.' She sat opposite him, and lifted up her voice, and wept."

Brothers and sisters — "about a bow shot away". She walked to the exact distance at which she could still see him and could no longer hear him crying. That is the outer limit of what a mother can bear.
Verse 17: "God heard the voice of the boy."
Look hard at that sentence. The text has just told us that Hagar lifted up her voice and wept — and what God says is: I have heard the voice of the boy.

Why? Because that child's name is Ishmael, יִשְׁמָעֵאל (*Yishmael*) — and the name means "God hears". Fourteen years earlier, beside another well, God had given him that name himself. And now, on the thirstiest day of his life, the name is honoured.
And verse 19 is my favourite verse in the whole chapter: "God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water."
Brothers and sisters, that well was already there. God did not dig a new well. He opened her eyes.

Sometimes what we are asking for is a change in the circumstances, and what God gives is a pair of eyes that have been opened. Those two things sound a long way apart, and the outcome is the same — she had water to drink.
Sarah wanted Hagar and her son driven out, and God actually tells Abraham to listen to her. How is that fair?

This passage has to be handled with care. The text is very honest about it: the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight, because that boy was his son too. What God says to him has two parts. First, "Don't let it be grievous in your sight because of the boy, and because of your servant"; and second, "For your offspring will be named through Isaac" — and then straight afterwards, "I will also make a nation of the son of the servant, because he is your child." So God has not abandoned them. This passage is not an endorsement of Sarah's motives; it is God dealing with a situation in which two households can no longer live together, and taking personal responsibility for the party who is being sent out. Paul does use this episode in Galatians 4 to draw a contrast between two covenants, but that is a figurative use of the story, not a certificate of approval for driving people out.
"God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water" — was the well there all along?

What the text says is that God "opened her eyes" — that is the literal Hebrew — and it does not say that God created a well on the spot. So the reading most interpreters take is this: the well was already there, and in her despair she could not see it. And that is intensely practical for us, because when a person is breaking down, the field of vision narrows until nothing is left in it but the trouble. In verse 16 she puts the child under one of the shrubs and walks away about a bow shot, saying, "Don't let me see the death of the child" — that is the picture of a mother who has come to the very end. And the first thing God does is not to rebuke her weakness. It is to make her eyes see. If there is someone beside you in that condition, this is your work too: stay with him, until he can see the well.
From verse 22 to the end of the chapter the scene changes again. Abimelech arrives with the captain of his army and says to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do."

Brothers and sisters, notice who is saying it — the king from the previous chapter, the one he lied to. A foreigner whose whole household suffered because of what Abraham did comes back and says: we can see it, God is with you.

And in the course of making the covenant, Abraham does something rather out of character. Verse 25: "Abraham complained to Abimelech because of a water well, which Abimelech's servants had violently taken away."

He raised the complaint. Brothers and sisters, this is the man who in chapter 13 handed his nephew the whole plain without a word, and here he speaks up over one well. This is exactly the distinction we drew before: over possessions you can yield; over what is right you have to speak. And he does not fall out with the man — he puts the matter plainly on the table, and then he makes a covenant.
Verse 33: "Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba, and there he called on the name of Yahweh, the Everlasting God."

Brothers and sisters, planting a tree is a very slow act. A tamarisk grows extremely slowly; it takes decades before it gives any shade. A man well past a hundred plants a tree that will take decades to give shade — he is not planting it for himself.

And the name "the Everlasting God", אֵל עוֹלָם (*El Olam*), appears here for the first time in the Bible. A man who knows he will not live to sit in the shade of his own tree calls on the name of the God who is forever.
God heard "the voice of the boy", not Hagar's weeping. What is that meant to tell us?

Verse 17: "God heard the voice of the boy. The angel of God called to Hagar out of the sky, and said to her, 'What troubles you, Hagar? Don't be afraid.'" It is remarkable — the text says the voice God heard was the child's, and the one he speaks to is the mother. That tells us two things. First, God hears the one who is least able to speak up for himself. Second, God's comfort very often arrives through his speaking to the carer. And the name Ishmael itself simply means "God hears". So at the lowest moment of Hagar's life, the answer had been hanging on her son's name the whole time; she had only forgotten it. Which is a reminder to us: write down the signs God has given you in the past while you still remember them, because at the point of despair people forget.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching the casting out of the servant as though God did not want Ishmael. In verses 13 and 20 God says plainly that he will bless that boy and make a nation of him; 17:20 says, "Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly." Preach it as rejection and you have turned God's mercy upside down.

The second is using the picture in Galatians 4 to look down on any modern people group. What Paul is contrasting there is two kinds of life — the one born of the flesh and the one born through the promise. It is a spiritual contrast, not a rating of ethnic groups. Misuse it and you manufacture hatred.

The third is preaching "twenty-five years of waiting" as though waiting long enough guarantees that you will get it. Sarah's waiting had God's explicit promise standing in front of it; that is not a general formula. Preach it as a guarantee and the people who never received will conclude that they did not wait hard enough or believe hard enough. Hebrews 11:13 says of these very people, "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar."

The fourth is preaching Isaac's laughter and skipping the weeping in the wilderness. In one chapter there is a great feast, and there is also a mother holding a child who is dying of thirst. Scripture set the two scenes side by side on purpose. If you preach only the joy, the people who are weeping will conclude that this chapter is not about them.

The fifth is brushing past Abraham's grief in a single line. Verse 11 says the thing was very grievous in his sight, and the Hebrew is extremely heavy. A man who obeys is not a man who feels nothing. Preach obedience as though it comes without a struggle, and the next time your congregation is struggling they will conclude that they are simply not spiritual enough.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: I have prayed about one thing for years and nothing has moved — how do I tell the difference between "the set time has not come" and "God has said no"? Brothers and sisters, let me answer this one honestly: very often you cannot tell, and Scripture does not hand us a formula for deciding. But I can give you three practical directions. First, look at whether there is a clear word. Behind Sarah's waiting stood an explicit promise from God — he said it three separate times. Is the thing you are waiting for something God has spoken, or something you are hoping for? You may ask for both, but they do not carry the same weight. Second, look at who the waiting is turning you into. Twenty-five years did not make Abraham bitter; they taught him to call on the name of the Everlasting God. If your waiting is making you harder and more closed off year by year, then the thing that needs dealing with may not be the request at all — it may be the bitterness. Third, and most important of all: whether or not you can tell the difference, you may keep asking, and you may say "but if not" at the same time. The three men in Daniel 3 said, "But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods." That phrase — "but if not" — is a mark of faith that has grown up.

The second question: Chinese families often run a particular arrangement, in which one child is sacrificed, sent away, or required to make way for another child. What does what happens to Hagar and Ishmael in this chapter say to a person like that? Brothers and sisters, I want to say this one very gently, and very seriously. The gentle part: I will not use the sentence "this was God's arrangement" to dispose of anybody who has been sacrificed. Coming out of a bystander's mouth, that sentence is cruel. The serious part: look at what God actually does in this chapter. He does not pretend it did not hurt — the text records the whole of it, the water in the container running out, the mother walking away about a bow shot, the weeping out loud. And then he does three things. He hears the boy's voice. He says to her, "Get up, lift up the boy, and hold him with your hand." And he opens her eyes. And verse 20 says, "God was with the boy, and he grew." Brothers and sisters, if you are the child who was sent away, this chapter wants you to know: God went out into the wilderness with you. He did not stay behind on the side where the feast was.
A relationship in my family has reached the point where we cannot live together. Does separating simply mean I have failed?

Not necessarily. Some relationships have to be repaired and some have to have their distance adjusted, and this chapter is an example of the second kind — carried out, moreover, in the presence of God. Watch three things. First, separating does not mean cutting off provision: Abraham gave bread and a container of water; it was not much, but he did not send them away empty-handed. Second, separating does not mean God stops caring: God himself went after the party who had been sent away. Third, if the separation involves safety and harm, protection comes first, and you must seek help from outside. And one practical reminder: after a separation, do not talk about the other person behind their back. That is the single easiest way to turn one adjustment into a lifetime of hatred.
7. Living 321 Out — Doing the Things That Only Give Shade in Ten Years
Brothers and sisters, let us take this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — in verse 18 God says, "Get up, lift up the boy, and hold him with your hand." He does not only give comfort; he gives an action. And in Mark 2:11 the Lord Jesus says to the paralytic, "I tell you, arise, take up your mat, and go to your house." Brothers and sisters, this is my role model: his comfort always comes with something that gets a person back on his feet. So when we go to comfort somebody, alongside sitting with them, we give them — at the right moment — one next step they can actually take.

The Bible is my standard — in this chapter one piece of commentary appears for the second time: "as God had commanded him". If a man's whole life can have that sentence written over it twice, three times, that is enough. A standard is not there to make you right every single time. It is there so that time after time you come back to the same sentence.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — verse 19: "God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water." Brothers and sisters, this is one of the most characteristic shapes of the Spirit's work. He very often does not change your situation; he changes what you are able to see. Ephesians 1:18 speaks of "having the eyes of your hearts enlightened". What you need most this week may not be a new answer. It may be a pair of eyes that have been opened.

Let Jesus be King — in verse 12 God says, "In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice", and verse 11 has already told us that the thing was very grievous in his sight. He obeyed. He obeyed with tears in his eyes. Brothers and sisters, letting Jesus be King includes the obedience that comes with tears. Obedience does not have to wait until you have thought it all through and your heart is at peace before it counts.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — what Sarah says is "God has made me laugh", not "I finally got through it". And what Abimelech says is "God is with you in all that you do". Even the foreigner put the glory in the right place.

Establish God's system — he planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and called on the name of the Everlasting God. Brothers and sisters, planting a tree is a very slow act, and the tree he planted was one whose shade he would never sit in. To establish God's system is to do the things that only give shade in ten years: leading a small group for five years, walking with one young person for ten, praying about one matter for twenty. None of those things show a result at the time.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We put a great deal of weight on overcoming, on breakthrough, on revival — and this chapter reminds us that inside one single chapter there are people throwing a feast and a woman weeping in the wilderness. If our meetings only keep a seat for the testimony of the one who has come through, then the people who are still out in the wilderness have nowhere to sit down. A healthy community has to be able to hold the great laugh of verse 6 and the loud weeping of verse 16 at the same time — because that is exactly how Scripture itself writes it.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Well
Brothers and sisters, four kinds of heart, and one and the same wilderness. And it was there that God opened eyes, and opened a well.

The proud heart says: "Sarah got there in the end, because she was the one with the promise." A heart like that finishes this chapter and files itself on the side of the feast. Brothers and sisters, notice that half of this chapter is taken up with the wilderness. The author put the two scenes side by side precisely so that you could not stand on only one side of it.

The fearful heart says: "My container of water is nearly finished." A heart like that starts to panic the moment it counts its resources. And here is what I want to say to it: look at verse 19. That well was already there before the container ran dry. Your supply is not the same thing as your container. And notice too when God opened her eyes — it was after the water was spent. That part is hard, and it is true.

The ashamed heart says: "I am the one who was thrown out." And you may genuinely have been asked to leave — by a group, by a family, by a church. Brothers and sisters, look at verse 17: "The angel of God called to Hagar out of the sky, and said to her, 'What troubles you, Hagar? Don't be afraid.'" God called her by her name — and this is the second time. Once beside the well in chapter 16, and once again out in the wilderness in chapter 21. The woman other people sent away is called by name by God, and called twice.

The wounded heart says: "Why did God make her send the child away?" I am not going to dodge that one. The text does say God endorsed that decision; and the text also lets us know that this whole situation was produced by a human arrangement back in chapter 16. Brothers and sisters, God sometimes makes his decisions inside wreckage that people have created, and when he decides, he does not drop a single one of them — he went out into the wilderness with the child who was sent away, and he promised to make him a nation. That does not make the pain of the moment any smaller. But it does tell you this: God was not standing on the side of the people who sent you away.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, write down the one thing you are waiting for, and write beside it: "at the set time of which God has spoken". You do not have to pretend you are sure. Just put that sentence next to it, where it will catch your eye every day.

Second, ask for a pair of eyes that have been opened. Turn your prayer in a different direction this week: instead of asking for the circumstances to change, ask first, "Lord, let me see what is already here." And then write down what you see.

Third, plant a tree. Do one thing that will only give shade in ten years: start walking with one person, start praying regularly about one matter, start writing a notebook meant for your children. The thing that shows no result today is the thing that is actually a tree.

Fourth, go and take a look at the wilderness side. Think this week about whether there is somebody near you who is weeping while everybody else is off at a feast somewhere. Send him a message, or simply go and sit beside him.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences: there is a woman in the Bible who waited twenty-five years before her child was born, and Scripture says that was not lateness, that was "the set time of which God had spoken"; in that same chapter another mother out in the wilderness ran out of water, put her child under a bush and walked away, because she could not bear to watch him die; and what God did was not to conjure up a new well — he opened her eyes so that she saw the one that had been there all along.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that my waiting is not being forgotten; it is that the day has not yet come, and he has remembered all along.
I declare that I am not only asking for my circumstances to change; I am asking, more than that, for a pair of eyes that have been opened.
I declare that I will obey even with tears in my eyes; obedience does not have to wait until I have worked it all out before it counts.
I declare that I will do the things that only give shade in ten years, because the God I serve is the Everlasting God.
This week I am supposed to speak out one testimony, but I am afraid people will think I am showing off.

The difference shows up in three places. First, who is the subject: the subject of a testimony should be God and not me — swap "what I did" for "what God did". Second, whether the hard part is left in: a story that is all outcome sounds like an advertisement, and only when you tell the waiting part as well can people catch hold of it. Third, what the listener walks away with: a good testimony makes people trust God too; it does not make them envy you. Sarah's line, "Everyone who hears will laugh with me", is exactly that standard — her testimony is meant to make other people laugh, not to make them feel small. In practice, write three sentences first: what I was waiting for at the time, what was going on inside me, and what God did afterwards. Read them out as written; you do not have to improvise.
Brothers and sisters, if only two pictures from this lesson can remain, I want to set them side by side.

The first picture: a hundred-year-old man holding his son, a great feast spread outside the tent, and Sarah laughing and saying to every single person who comes, "God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me."

The second picture: under the same sky, out towards the wilderness of Beersheba, a woman putting her child under a bush, walking away about a bow shot, sitting down and lifting up her voice and weeping, because the water in the container was spent.
Brothers and sisters, both of those scenes are in the same chapter. The author did not file them separately.
And God did two things in this chapter: he made a woman who had waited twenty-five years laugh out loud, and out in the wilderness he heard the voice of a child.

Look again at that sentence in verse 17: "God heard the voice of the boy." And the child's name means exactly that — God hears. The name God gave him fourteen years earlier was honoured on the thirstiest day of his life.

Brothers and sisters, if today you are on the side where the feast is, remember that the laughter was made by God and not ground out by you. If today you are on the side where the wilderness is, remember that God came out there with you, and that he knows your name.
And that well — it was already there.

The focus is not on how long I have waited, not on whether I am at the feast or in the wilderness, and not on how much water is left in my container. The focus is on Jesus — he is the One who hears, the One who calls a person by name, the One who opens eyes. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us: this week, ask for a pair of eyes that have been opened, and plant a tree whose shade you will never live to sit in. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road that runs downward. The first drives the point of this lesson into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ The text does not say "at last"; it says only "at the set time of which God had spoken". How does that way of putting it change the way you look at waiting?
2. ★★★ One and the same word for laughter turns from the laugh of unbelief into the laugh of joy. God did not take the laugh away; he only changed what was inside it. What hope does that give you?
3. ★ The well was already there; what God did was open Hagar's eyes. What does that give us to understand about not being able to see anything when we are in despair?
4. ★★ The voice God heard was the boy's, and the one he spoke to was the mother. What does that arrangement show you about God?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I am the one who got through it), fearful (what if it falls through again), ashamed (I laughed once; I do not deserve it), wounded (I am the one who was sent away). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there nothing left in your field of vision at the moment except one difficulty? If God opened your eyes, what do you think you would see first?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The one thing God has done for me this year is …"
9. ★★ This week, who are you going to tell that to? Name the person, the time and the setting.

Leader's reminder: question nine will touch on the experience of coming to the end of one's strength. If someone speaks about a time when he could not carry on, stay with him first; do not hurry to hand him a verse. If thoughts of self-harm are involved, be sure to follow up with him privately after the meeting and help him find professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own household, is there someone who is walking out to the place "about a bow shot away"? How will you stay with him this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, who needs somebody to open his eyes for him?
12. ★★★ The practice of writing down the signs: this week, write down three things God has done for you in the past, and keep them somewhere you can find them. Say where you are going to write them.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and tell your testimony to him first, once, this week. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is an old woman in the Bible who once laughed because she did not believe. Second, after the child was born she said, "God has made me laugh", and said that everyone who heard would laugh along with her. Third, so I believe that God will not take my laughter away; he will change what is inside it. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: who you will tell your testimony to this week, and which person you will stay with. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to open our eyes to see the well that is already there.
